subject: History
source: National Curriculum KS2 (Britain's settlement by Anglo-Saxons and Scots; the Viking and Anglo-Saxon struggle for the Kingdom of England); no school Drive history material found for Y5, written from scratch | Spring 1 2027 (lessons 5 to 9): Tarbiyyah Primary Year 5 curriculum map and History Long Term Plan 2023-24 (Cornerstones Dynamic Dynasties: early civilisations and Shang China); TGA Year 5 pack

lessons.title: The Anglo-Saxons arrive
objectives: Explain why the Anglo-Saxons came to Britain
Locate the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms on a map

keywords.def: people from the Angles, Saxons and Jutes who settled in Britain
to make a home in a new place
a land ruled by a king or queen
moving from one place to live in another

starter: Around which year did the Romans leave Britain?
What does the word legacy mean?

teach.heading: Bismillah: after the Romans
bullets: Settlers came across the North Sea
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Recap Year 4 learning on the Romans. Ask: what might happen to a country when its army leaves? Collect ideas.

teach.heading: Who were they?
bullets: They came from Denmark and northern Germany
teach.note: The Angles gave England its name (Angle-land). Use a map to show the sea crossing. Explain that Anglo-Saxon settlement happened gradually, over many years, in the fifth and sixth centuries.

teach.heading: Why did they come?
bullets: Their homes flooded or were crowded
Some may have been invited as soldiers
teach.note: Historians suggest several reasons. Stress we cannot be certain: our evidence is limited because few written records survive. Link to why people migrate today.

teach.heading: Seven kingdoms
bullets: Kingdoms included Wessex, Mercia and Northumbria
teach.note: Show a map of the main kingdoms: Northumbria, Mercia, East Anglia, Essex, Kent, Sussex, Wessex. Mention the old name 'Heptarchy'. Ask pupils where they live and which kingdom it was.

practice: Where did the Anglo-Saxons come from?
Name two reasons they came to Britain.
independent: Label a map of Anglo-Saxon England with six kingdoms
Draw arrows showing where the Angles, Saxons and Jutes came from
Write a paragraph beginning 'The Anglo-Saxons came to Britain because ...'
exit: Which group gave England its name?
lessons.homework: Find out where the name of your area or nearby town comes from; some end in -ham, -ton or -ley from Old English.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: pre-labelled map to colour and a word bank. Stretch: explain why historians find it hard to be sure why the Anglo-Saxons came.

lessons.title: Anglo-Saxon life, Sutton Hoo and Christianity
objectives: Describe life in an Anglo-Saxon village
Explain what Sutton Hoo tells us about Anglo-Saxon society

keywords.def: a nobleman who served the king
a site in Suffolk with a royal ship burial
studying the past through objects and sites
a person sent to spread a religion

starter: Which three groups made up the Anglo-Saxons?
Why does moving house or country happen?

teach.heading: Village life
bullets: Villages had wooden halls and small huts
Families made clothes, tools and pots
teach.note: Show a reconstruction of West Stow village. Compare Roman towns with Anglo-Saxon villages. Misconception: Anglo-Saxons were less skilled; they made fine metalwork and jewellery.

teach.heading: Sutton Hoo
bullets: A ship burial of a king, probably Raedwald
It held gold, silver and a helmet
teach.note: Sutton Hoo is dated to around AD 625 and the person is usually thought to be King Raedwald of East Anglia. Say 'probably'. Show the helmet. The ship had rotted, leaving an impression in the sand.

teach.heading: What the evidence shows
bullets: Rich objects came from far away
The king had power and trade links
It challenges the idea of a 'dark age'
teach.note: Garnets from India or Sri Lanka and silver from the Byzantine Empire were found. Ask what this suggests about contact with the wider world, including the Muslim world later, through trade.

teach.heading: Christianity arrives
bullets: Pope Gregory sent Augustine in AD 597
Augustine met King Ethelbert in Kent
teach.note: Keep to the facts. Anglo-Saxons had earlier followed pagan gods like Woden and Thor, remembered in Wednesday and Thursday. Treat all religions respectfully.

practice: What was found at Sutton Hoo?
Why is the ship burial important to historians?
What was a monastery used for?
independent: Draw an Anglo-Saxon village with labels
Write a museum label for the Sutton Hoo helmet
Explain what Sutton Hoo tells us about the king in 5 sentences
exit: Name two things found in the Sutton Hoo burial.
Who brought Christianity to Kent in AD 597?
lessons.homework: Find out which day of the week is named after an Anglo-Saxon god and write the name of the god.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: museum label starters and a picture bank. Stretch: say what is still unknown about Sutton Hoo.

lessons.title: Viking raiders
objectives: Explain who the Vikings were and where they came from
Describe the Viking raid on Lindisfarne in AD 793

keywords.def: a seafaring people from Scandinavia who raided and settled lands
the region of Norway, Sweden and Denmark
a long, narrow Viking boat with oars and a sail
a community of monks who live and pray together

starter: Name a famous Anglo-Saxon burial site.
Who brought Christianity to Kent in AD 597?
Which kingdom was Sutton Hoo in?

teach.heading: Who were the Vikings?
bullets: Vikings came from Norway, Sweden and Denmark
They were farmers, traders and raiders
Their boats let them cross seas quickly
teach.note: Bismillah. Challenge the stereotype that Vikings were only raiders with horned helmets; there is no evidence they wore horned helmets. Show a longship picture.

teach.heading: Why leave home?
bullets: Viking kings wanted power and wealth
teach.note: Use 'historians suggest'. Ask pupils to rank reasons: which seems most convincing? Link to migration reasons last lesson.

teach.heading: Lindisfarne, AD 793
bullets: Vikings attacked a monastery on Lindisfarne
It is an island off Northumbria
Monks were killed and treasure was stolen
teach.note: This is the first well-known Viking raid, recorded in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle. Remember the Chronicle was written by monks, so sources could be biased. Show the island on a map.

teach.heading: Raiders become settlers
bullets: Vikings began to settle and farm
teach.note: Explain the shift from raiding to settlement. Pupils should note not all Vikings were violent; many traded peacefully. Include Viking trade routes reaching Baghdad, where silver coins were exchanged (link to Year 6).

practice: Where did the Vikings come from?
Why might the monks' accounts be one-sided?
independent: Draw and label a Viking longship
Write a newspaper report: 'Raid on Lindisfarne, AD 793'
Make a mind map of reasons the Vikings came to Britain
exit: What happened at Lindisfarne in AD 793?
Give one reason why a monk's account might be biased.
lessons.homework: Find three Viking words in English (e.g. sky, egg, knife) and note their meanings.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: newspaper template with headline word bank. Stretch: compare two reasons for Viking raids and say which is stronger.

lessons.title: Alfred the Great and the Danelaw
objectives: Explain how Alfred of Wessex resisted the Vikings

keywords.def: the part of England ruled by the Vikings under their law
a formal agreement between two sides
the Anglo-Saxon kingdom in the south of England
a fortified Anglo-Saxon town

starter: What does a longship look like?

teach.heading: Vikings take land
bullets: By AD 870 the Vikings controlled most kingdoms
teach.note: Bismillah. Point out Northumbria, East Anglia and most of Mercia fell. Alfred was the youngest brother; ask pupils how it feels to lead in a crisis.

teach.heading: Battle of Edington
bullets: In AD 878 Alfred beat the Viking leader Guthrum
teach.note: Mention the story of Alfred and the cakes is a legend, not proven fact. Ask: why is it useful to tell legends from evidence?

teach.heading: The Danelaw
bullets: Vikings ruled the north and east
Alfred ruled the south and west
teach.note: Show the line on a map. 'Dane law' means areas where Viking law applied. Place names ending in -by and -thorpe show Viking settlement.

teach.heading: Alfred's reforms
bullets: He built ships and organised an army
teach.note: Alfred valued education and had books translated into English. Link to the idea in Islam of seeking knowledge. Alfred died in AD 899; his grandson Athelstan became the first king of all England in AD 927.

practice: Which place-name endings show Viking influence?
independent: Colour a map of England showing the Danelaw and Wessex
Write a short profile of Alfred explaining why he is called 'the Great'
List three things you would do to defend a town from raiders
exit: Which battle did Alfred win in AD 878?
Give one reason Alfred is called 'the Great'.
lessons.homework: Find a place near you or in England that ends in -by or -thorpe and say what you think it means.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: pre-drawn map outline with key words to attach. Stretch: judge whether Alfred deserved the title 'the Great' using three pieces of evidence.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Early river civilisations and Shang China (Dynamic Dynasties)
lessons.title: The first river civilisations
lessons.bigQuestion: Why did the first great civilisations all grow up beside rivers?
objectives: To understand where and when the earliest civilisations began and why rivers mattered
successCriteria: All: name four early river civilisations
Most: place them on a timeline and a map
Some: explain why rivers helped civilisations grow

keywords.def: a large, organised society with towns, rulers and writing
a line of rulers from the same family
events in time order
good for growing crops
before year 1, counting backwards

hook.text: If you were choosing where to build the first city, what would you look for?

islamicLink.text: Allah tells us: 'Travel through the land and see how was the end of those before you' (ar-Rum 30:42). Learning about ancient civilisations helps us reflect on how people lived, ruled and believed, and what lasted.

starter.q: Which is longer ago: 3000 BC or 1000 BC?

starter.a: A large, organised society with towns, rulers and writing

teach.heading: Four river civilisations
teach.note: Show each river on the world map.

teach.heading: When?
teach.note: Dates are approximate.

teach.heading: Why rivers?
bullets: Water to drink and for crops
teach.note: Ask: which of these would matter most to you?

teach.heading: Finding ancient China
bullets: The Yellow River flows east to the sea
teach.note: Show the Yellow River on a map of China.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: Which civilisation grew up beside the Yellow River?
check.why: Egypt is on the Nile; Sumer on the Tigris and Euphrates; Shang China on the Yellow River.

practice.q: Which river did ancient Egypt grow beside?
practice.model:
Look at the four rivers.
Egypt matches the Nile.
So the answer is the Nile.

practice.q: Which began first: Shang China or Sumer?
Give one reason rivers helped civilisations.
practice.a: For example: water for crops, fertile soil or trade

independent.q: Core: Make a timeline of the four civilisations and label each river on a world map.
independent.a: Sumer about 3500 BC (Tigris and Euphrates); Egypt about 3100 BC (Nile); Indus about 2600 BC (Indus); Shang about 1600 BC (Yellow River)
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: line from 4000 BC to 1000 BC, mark 3500 BC 'Sumer', then find the Tigris on the map.

independent.q: Extend: Write a sentence explaining why the first cities grew by rivers.
independent.a: They had water, fertile soil for farming and a way to travel and trade

independent.q: Stretch: How many years after Sumer's first cities did the Shang dynasty begin?

exit.a: A line of rulers from one family
options: A line of rulers from one family

exit.q: Big question: why did the first great civilisations all grow up beside rivers?
exit.a: Rivers gave water, fertile soil for food and routes for trade

lessons.homework: Find the Yellow River on a map or globe and trace it from the mountains to the sea.
lessons.send: SEND: timeline cards to order. EAL: river, city, farm, trade. Stretch: find out what 'Mesopotamia' means (land between rivers).

Atlas or online map shared on screen

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Early river civilisations and Shang China (Dynamic Dynasties)
lessons.title: The Yellow River and the Shang kingdom
lessons.bigQuestion: Was the Yellow River a friend or an enemy to the Shang?
objectives: To understand how the Yellow River shaped the Shang kingdom
successCriteria: All: locate the Yellow River and the Shang lands
Most: describe how the river helped and harmed people
Some: explain why the river is sometimes called 'China's Sorrow'
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: trust in Allah and wise planning

keywords.def: a long river in northern China, also called the Huang He
fine mud carried by a river
the dynasty that ruled northern China about 1600 to 1046 BC
when water spills over the land
a grain crop grown by the Shang

hook.text: Why might a river that floods often still be a good place to live?

islamicLink.text: Allah lists the rain that He sends down from the sky, giving life to the earth, among His signs (al-Baqarah 2:164). Muslims are taught to work hard, plan wisely and trust in Allah, as the Shang farmers had to plan for floods.

starter.q: Which came first: Sumer or Shang?

teach.heading: The Yellow River
bullets: Flows to the sea in the east
teach.note: The silt is fine yellow soil called loess, washed into the river. It gives the river its colour.

teach.heading: A friend
teach.note: Shang farmers grew millet, and later rice in wetter places.

teach.heading: An enemy
teach.note: Rulers had to organise people to build banks and channels.

teach.heading: The Shang kingdom
teach.note: Archaeologists found Yin near the modern city of Anyang.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: Why is the Yellow River yellow?
check.why: Fine yellow soil (loess) is washed into it.

practice.q: Give one way the river helped the Shang.
practice.a: For example: fertile silt for crops
practice.model:
Think: what do farmers need?
Good soil.
The river leaves fertile silt.
So it helped them farm.

practice.q: Give one way the river harmed the Shang.
What was the last Shang capital?

independent.q: Core: Make a 'friend or enemy' table for the Yellow River with three points each side.
independent.a: Friend: silt, water, fish/transport. Enemy: floods, changing course, lost crops
independent.model: Teacher shows row 1: 'Friend: leaves fertile silt. Enemy: floods destroy homes.'

independent.q: Extend: Write a paragraph answering the big question. Use the portal response box.
independent.a: For example: It was both. It gave fertile soil, but its floods destroyed homes, so the Shang had to manage it

independent.q: Stretch: How is the Yellow River like the Nile for Egypt?
independent.a: Both flooded and left fertile soil that let farming and cities grow

exit.a: Fine mud carried by a river
options: Fine mud carried by a river

exit.q: Big question: was the Yellow River a friend or an enemy to the Shang?
exit.a: Both: it brought fertile soil and water but also deadly floods

lessons.homework: Make a diagram of the Yellow River with labels for 'friend' and 'enemy' features.
lessons.send: SEND: picture cards to sort into friend or enemy. EAL: flood, farm, mud. Stretch: research how people control floods today.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Early river civilisations and Shang China (Dynamic Dynasties)
lessons.title: Shang kings, ancestors and bronze
lessons.bigQuestion: How do bronze objects help us understand the Shang?
objectives: To understand how the Shang made bronze and what their bronzes tell us
successCriteria: All: say what bronze is made from
Most: describe how the Shang cast bronze
Some: use bronze objects as evidence about Shang society
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: metals as gifts from Allah

keywords.def: a metal made by mixing copper and tin
pour hot liquid metal into a mould
a hollow shape that liquid sets in
a family member from long ago
an object made by people in the past

hook.text: If archaeologists only found your family's most precious objects, what would they guess about you?

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'And We sent down iron, in which is great strength and benefits for people' (al-Hadid 57:25). Metals are gifts from Allah. The Shang used bronze to show the power of their kings; Muslims are taught to use wealth and skill to please Allah, not to show off.

starter.q: Why is the Yellow River called 'China's Sorrow'?

teach.heading: Shang kings
teach.note: We learn about Shang beliefs as history. Muslims worship Allah alone and do not pray to ancestors.

teach.heading: What is bronze?
teach.note: Copper and tin were dug from the ground as ores and melted.

teach.heading: Casting bronze
teach.note: Shang workers made clay moulds in several pieces.
cycle: Make a clay mould around it

teach.heading: Bronzes as evidence
teach.note: One Shang bronze vessel weighs over 800 kg. Ask: what does this tell us about the Shang? They were organised and skilled.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.why: Bronze is copper and tin. Iron came later in China.

practice.a: Pour hot liquid metal into a mould
practice.model:
Read the keyword.
Cast: pour melted metal into a mould.
When it cools it takes the mould's shape.

practice.q: What does a huge bronze vessel tell us about the Shang?
practice.a: They were wealthy, organised and skilled

independent.q: Core: Draw and label the steps of casting a Shang bronze vessel (five steps).
independent.a: Clay model, clay mould, pour bronze, cool, break mould and polish
independent.model: Teacher shows step 1: a clay pot shape labelled 'make a clay model'.

independent.q: Extend: Write what bronze objects tell us about Shang society.
independent.a: Skilled workers, rich and powerful rulers, important ceremonies

independent.q: Stretch: Why are objects from tombs good evidence but not the whole story?
independent.a: They show rich people's lives, not ordinary farmers'

exit.a: An object made by people in the past
options: An object made by people in the past

exit.q: Big question: how do bronze objects help us understand the Shang?
exit.a: They show the Shang were skilled, organised and had rich, powerful rulers

lessons.homework: Make a clay or dough 'vessel' with a pattern pressed into it (patterns only, no faces).
lessons.send: SEND: casting steps as picture cards. EAL: melt, pour, cool, mould. Stretch: find out what a 'ding' vessel is.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Early river civilisations and Shang China (Dynamic Dynasties)
lessons.title: Oracle bones and early Chinese writing
lessons.bigQuestion: What can 3,000-year-old bones tell us about the Shang?
objectives: To understand what oracle bones are and how they show early Chinese writing
successCriteria: All: say what oracle bones are
Most: explain how the Shang used them
Some: explain why they are such important evidence
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: only Allah knows the future

keywords.def: a piece of bone or shell with writing, used to ask questions
writing cut into a hard surface
a written symbol in Chinese
a system of writing
someone who studies the past by digging up remains

hook.text: If you could only write ten words for people in 3,000 years to read, which would you choose?

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'With Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them except Him' (al-An'am 6:59). The Prophet, peace be upon him, warned Muslims not to go to fortune-tellers (Sahih Muslim). Instead of reading cracks in bones, a Muslim makes du'a and istikharah and trusts Allah.

starter.a: Pour hot metal into a mould

teach.heading: What are oracle bones?
bullets: Ox shoulder bones and turtle shells
teach.note: Shang kings asked about harvests, weather, wars and illness.

teach.heading: How they were used
bullets: Heat the bone until it cracked
Read the cracks as an answer
teach.note: This was fortune-telling. We study it as history; Islam teaches that only Allah knows the unseen.

teach.heading: The earliest Chinese writing
bullets: Oldest large body of Chinese writing
teach.note: Show examples: the character for 'sun' began as a circle with a dot.

teach.heading: Found in 1899
teach.note: This shows how an object's meaning can be lost and found again.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: Oracle bones are important evidence because they:
check.why: They are the oldest large body of Chinese writing and tell us what Shang kings worried about.

practice.q: What were oracle bones made from?
practice.a: Ox shoulder bones and turtle shells
practice.model:
Read the first slide.
They were bones and shells.
Ox shoulder bones and turtle shells.

practice.q: Name one thing Shang kings asked about.
practice.a: For example: harvests, weather, war or illness

practice.q: When were oracle bones recognised as writing?

independent.q: Core: Write five facts about oracle bones in a fact file. Use the portal response box or your book.
independent.a: Made of ox bones and turtle shells; questions carved; heated to crack; earliest Chinese writing; found in 1899
independent.model: Teacher shows fact 1: 'Oracle bones were ox shoulder bones or turtle shells.'

independent.q: Extend: What do the questions tell us about Shang worries?
independent.a: They worried about food, weather, war and health

independent.q: Stretch: Why does Islam forbid fortune-telling, and how should a Muslim face worries instead?
independent.a: Only Allah knows the unseen; a Muslim makes du'a, plans wisely and trusts Allah

exit.a: Writing cut into a hard surface
options: Writing cut into a hard surface

exit.q: Big question: what can 3,000-year-old bones tell us about the Shang?
exit.a: Their writing, their worries (harvests, war, weather) and how kings ruled

lessons.homework: Copy the four characters (sun, moon, tree, mountain) and explain each to your family.
lessons.send: SEND: fact file frame with picture prompts. EAL: bone, shell, write, question. Stretch: compare oracle bone writing with Egyptian hieroglyphs.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Early river civilisations and Shang China (Dynamic Dynasties)
lessons.title: The end of the Shang: comparing Egypt and Shang China
lessons.bigQuestion: How were ancient Egypt and Shang China alike, and how were they different?
objectives: To understand how the Shang dynasty ended and compare it with ancient Egypt
successCriteria: All: say who replaced the Shang and roughly when
Most: give two similarities between Egypt and Shang China
Some: write a comparison with evidence from both
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: all earthly power is temporary

keywords.def: the dynasty that replaced the Shang
the Zhou idea that a ruler's right to rule could be lost
what is left behind for the future
something that is the same
something that is not the same

hook.text: Do all powerful kingdoms end in the end? Why do you think so?

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'You give kingship to whom You will and take it from whom You will' (Al Imran 3:26). Every dynasty, from the pharaohs to the Shang, ended. Only Allah's kingdom lasts for ever.

starter.q: Oracle bones show the earliest Chinese:
Which river was ancient Egypt beside?

teach.heading: The Shang fall
bullets: Defeated by the Zhou at Muye
The Zhou ruled for centuries after
teach.note: The Zhou king Wu defeated the last Shang king.

teach.heading: The Mandate of Heaven
bullets: A bad ruler loses the right to rule
teach.note: Islam teaches that Allah gives power to whom He wills and takes it from whom He wills (Al Imran 3:26).

teach.heading: Egypt and Shang compared
teach.note: Pupils add ideas in the chat.

teach.heading: How to compare
teach.note: Model a comparison sentence.

model.problem: Compare writing in Egypt and Shang China
steps: Difference: hieroglyphs vs oracle bone script
model.answer: Both civilisations had writing, but Egypt used hieroglyphs whereas the Shang carved characters on oracle bones.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.why: The Zhou defeated the Shang in about 1046 BC.

practice.q: Write one similarity between Egypt and Shang China.
practice.a: For example: both grew beside a river that flooded
practice.model:
Pick a row: River.
Egypt: the Nile. Shang: the Yellow River.
Both grew beside rivers that flooded and left fertile soil.

practice.a: For example: Egypt had pharaohs and pyramids; Shang had kings and bronzes

independent.q: Core: Write a comparison paragraph of Egypt and Shang China using 'both', 'but' and 'whereas'. Use the portal response box.
independent.a: For example: Both grew beside rivers. Egypt had pharaohs, whereas the Shang had kings. Both had writing, but in different scripts.
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: 'Both Egypt and Shang China grew beside great rivers that flooded and left fertile soil.'

independent.q: Extend: Add one sentence about each civilisation's legacy.
independent.a: For example: Egypt left the pyramids; the Shang left the beginnings of Chinese writing

independent.q: Stretch: Which legacy matters more today? Give a reason.
independent.a: For example: Chinese writing, because over a billion people still use characters that grew from it

exit.a: What is left behind for the future
options: What is left behind for the future

exit.q: Big question: how were ancient Egypt and Shang China alike, and how were they different?
exit.a: Alike: river, rulers, writing, skilled crafts. Different: pharaohs and pyramids vs kings, bronzes and oracle bones

lessons.homework: Teach a family member three similarities and differences between Egypt and Shang China.
lessons.send: SEND: comparison frame with 'both' and 'but' starters. EAL: same, different, both, but. Stretch: add a third civilisation (Sumer) to your comparison.
